renderings.customer:
### What's New

- **Self-contained release binaries:** Preview releases now publish a self-contained, compressed binary for each supported platform. You no longer need the .NET runtime installed separately to run it.
- **Code-formatted identifiers:** Technical changelog entries now show command names, options, configuration keys, files, types and methods as code-formatted text, spelled exactly as they appear in the source. You can trust each formatted name to be accurate rather than guessed or shortened.
- **Provenance in changelog.json:** changelog.json can now include a provenance section recording the tool version, provider, model and prompt hash used to produce it. You can trace how a changelog was generated whenever that information is available, since any field with nothing to report is simply left out.
- **Default model and audiences:** Running without specifying a model now uses Claude Sonnet 5, and running without --audience now renders the technical and customer changelogs by default instead of all three. You can still render the product audience by naming it explicitly.
- **Where a release starts:** Generating a release that has no earlier tag to compare against now stops with an error instead of silently rendering your whole commit history as the release. Tell Chartula where the release starts with --since, or render the full history on purpose with --whole-history.
- **Draft release notes:** Generated release notes are now created as a draft on GitHub rather than published immediately. You can review and edit them before publishing, and re-running the same release updates that draft instead of creating a new one.
- **Default tag and repository:** Running chartula preview or generate from inside a git checkout now picks up the release tag and repository automatically, so you no longer have to pass --tag and --repo by hand. A defaulted value is printed before the run starts, and either flag can still be set explicitly.
- **Thinking-mode validation:** A thinking setting the configured Anthropic model doesn't support is now rejected when configuration loads, with a clear error, instead of only failing after fetching data and calling the model. You find out immediately if your thinking and model settings don't work together.
- **Consistent changelog structure:** Generated changelogs now use a fixed structure for headings, groups and breaking-change markers instead of leaving formatting to the model, so every run produces entries in the same shape. Every change now gets its own entry instead of being folded into a collapsed summary line.
- **Technical and product format:** Technical and product changelog entries now follow a fixed template instead of a format chosen by the model each time: technical entries are grouped as Changed, Added and Fixed with breaking changes listed first, and CHANGELOG.md sections now open with the version and date. Routine documentation, internal work and refactors are left out of these renderings unless labelled or marked breaking.
- **Labels in changelog.json:** changelog.json now includes the labels attached to each change, exactly as given on the pull request. Nothing in the generated changelogs changes yet, since what to do with the labels is decided elsewhere.
- **Selecting audiences to render:** You can now choose which audiences a run renders with --audience, naming one or more of technical, customer and product; leaving it out still renders all three. An output file is only written for an audience you actually render, and naming one that doesn't exist gives a clear error listing the valid ones.
- **Customer entry ordering:** Customer changelogs now list entries that need your action before ones that don't, with breaking changes always first, and nothing is added after the last group. Minor changes you wouldn't act on are gathered into a single closing note, and claims like faster or more reliable are only made when there's a number or basis to check them against.
- **GitHub token warning:** Running without a GitHub token set now prints a warning before the run starts, explaining that GitHub's lower rate limit can cause a release to fail partway through. You can set GITHUB_TOKEN to raise the limit, though the run still proceeds without it.
- **Customer release page:** A run now writes a release-\<tag>.md file containing the customer-facing changelog as a page you can publish, with a title, description and publish date included when available. A preview shows this description too, and no file is written when a release has no customer-facing entries.
- **Generating without publishing:** You can now run chartula generate --no-publish to write changelog.json and CHANGELOG.md without publishing release notes to GitHub; the run lists what it wrote and what it skipped. Without the flag, nothing changes: generate still writes and publishes everything as before.
- **OpenAI-compatible provider:** You can now set llm.provider to openai-compatible to use any endpoint speaking the OpenAI chat-completions dialect, including a server on your own machine, instead of only Anthropic. Both model and base URL must be set explicitly for this provider, and llm.baseUrl now also works with Anthropic for routing through a proxy.
- **Model thinking mode:** You can now set llm.thinking to provider-default, disabled or adaptive, instead of this being decided silently by whichever model you use. The default keeps today's behavior, so cost stays the same until you change it, and an unsupported combination for your model now fails clearly rather than being silently rejected.
- **Run cost metrics:** Every preview and generate run now ends with a summary of token usage and cost, broken down by rule-based check, thorough check and rephrasing. You can use the thorough-check line to judge whether its extra cost is finding anything the free check would have missed.
- **Category configuration:** You can now configure category order, display names and whether breaking changes are shown prominently in a categories section of chartula.yaml. An unknown category name is rejected at startup with a clear error listing the valid ones.
- **Configuration file:** chartula.yaml now lets you refine Chartula's behavior, covering the model, GitHub access, labels, filtering, fact-base depth, faithfulness checks and review, while the tool still works with no configuration file at all. An invalid value in the file is now reported as a clear configuration error instead of an unhandled exception.
- **Generate and preview commands:** chartula now has generate and preview commands, both taking --tag and --repo: generate produces and writes outputs including publishing release notes, while preview runs the same process but writes and publishes nothing. Errors during a run are now reported clearly instead of crashing the program.
- **GitHub release notes:** Generated changelog text can now be written directly to a release's GitHub notes instead of staying only in local files. Running again for the same tag updates that release's notes in place rather than creating a duplicate.
- **CHANGELOG.md history:** Each release is now written as a new section at the top of CHANGELOG.md, with earlier sections kept untouched below it. Running the same release again replaces its section in place instead of duplicating it or disturbing the order of history.
- **Review mode:** An optional review mode lets you approve or edit each generated text, with any flagged passages highlighted, before it's written. Review is off by default, so a run publishes straight through unless you turn it on.
- **Thorough faithfulness check:** A second, LLM-based check now reviews generated text against the facts for subtle, meaning-level errors that a simple rule-based check can't catch, such as a bug fix being rendered as something more dramatic. It's on by default, and you can disable it through configuration.
- **Rule-based faithfulness check:** A free, always-on check now flags invented numbers, quoted or backticked names, and breaking-change claims that don't appear in the source facts, before any AI-based check runs. It costs no tokens and runs on every release automatically.
- **Consistent multi-audience renderings:** Technical, customer and product-manager changelogs are now all generated from the same underlying set of facts, so they can't disagree about what changed. Customer omits internal-only changes, technical keeps full detail and links, and product groups changes by theme.
- **Rephrasing safeguards:** Generated changelog text is now built from a prompt that strictly rephrases the established facts rather than adding anything new, so a release with little detail gets a brief entry instead of invented padding. Categories and breaking-change flags are provided to the model rather than decided by it.
- **Changelog generation:** Chartula can now actually generate changelog text through the configured AI provider, making exactly one call per release instead of none. A provider failure is now reported clearly instead of crashing the tool, and a release with nothing to report makes no call at all.
- **Fact-base depth:** You can now choose how much source material feeds each change's description - title only, title plus pull request description (the default), or title, description and linked issues - to fit the way your team writes pull requests. This is set in the factBase section of chartula.yaml.
- **Release fact base:** Each curated pull request or commit is now turned into a structured fact, including category, breaking status and linked issues, that generated changelogs are built from. Linked issues are detected automatically from GitHub closing keywords like closes #12 in the title or body.
- **Changelog fact model:** Each change now carries a structured record of its established facts - title, pull request number and link, category, visibility and breaking flags, and linked issues - that the model may only rephrase from, never invent new details for.
- **Filtering internal changes:** Internal and chore-type changes are now left out of the changelog by default, so routine maintenance work doesn't clutter the entries. A breaking change is always kept regardless of its category, and you can change which categories are excluded in configuration.
- **Label-based curation rules:** GitHub labels can now steer curation: a label can exclude a pull request from the changelog, force it into a specific category, or restrict the changelog to only labelled pull requests. All of this is optional, so the tool works exactly as before if you don't use labels at all.
- **Change categorization:** Each change's category - feature, fix, performance, documentation, refactor, internal or other - is now decided deterministically from its Conventional Commit prefix before any AI involvement, so the model can never misclassify what kind of change something is. Breaking changes are tracked separately and flagged regardless of category.
- **Fallback for missing PR data:** When a release has no associated pull requests, or a pull request has a blank or uninformative title, the changelog now falls back to the commit message or the pull request description to describe that change. You can rely on a release never failing solely because pull request discipline was imperfect.
- **Pull request-based changelogs:** Changes are now summarized per merged pull request, using its title, description and labels, rather than per raw commit. API failures are reported with a clear error instead of crashing the tool.
- **Release commit range:** Chartula now determines exactly which commits belong to a release by reading the range since the previous tag, or the full history when there is no previous tag. Unknown or blank tags produce a clear error.
- **LLM provider support:** Chartula now generates changelog text through a provider-agnostic interface, starting with Anthropic as the first supported provider. API keys are read from configuration or environment variables rather than ever being hardcoded.

### What's Changed

- **Test tooling update:** Test tooling dependencies were updated to their latest versions.
- **Dependency updates:** Several underlying libraries, including the Anthropic and Microsoft.Extensions.AI packages, were updated to their latest versions.
- **Project scaffold:** The initial project structure, license and documentation were established as the starting point for this project.

### Bug Fixes

- **Reverted changes:** A pull request that reverted an earlier change in the same release could still be filtered out as internal work, leaving the reverted change announced in the changelog as if it had shipped. Reverted changes are now matched with what they undo and removed together, so you no longer see a change that was taken back before the release went out.
- **Truncated model responses:** A response cut short by the model provider, whether during changelog generation or the thorough faithfulness check, previously could pass through undetected, sometimes reported as a clean result. Chartula now checks that the full prompt could plausibly produce the reported token count and fails the run with a clear error instead.
- **Pull request description parsing:** A pull request description containing only hidden HTML comments or an unfilled template could previously be read as real content, including linking issues or flagging a change as breaking that the author never actually wrote. Hidden comments and empty templates are now treated as no description at all, so only what an author actually wrote is used.
- **Secure endpoint requirement:** Configuring a GitHub or AI provider endpoint with a plain http URL to a remote host previously went through, sending your credentials over an insecure connection as soon as the host was reachable. Such an endpoint is now refused at startup with a clear error; use https for remote endpoints, or http only for a local address like localhost.
- **Endpoint and credential configuration:** Setting the API endpoint URLs or the names of credential environment variables in chartula.yaml previously let a file in your repository silently redirect where release data and credentials get sent. These four settings can now only be set through environment variables, and a chartula.yaml that still sets one is refused at startup with a message naming the variable to use instead.
- **Git executable resolution:** Chartula previously could run a git executable placed inside the repository being analyzed rather than the real git on your system, letting a malicious checkout run arbitrary code with your environment and credentials. Git is now resolved once from your system PATH, and a machine without git installed is refused upfront with a clear error.
- **Draft release updates:** Updating an existing draft release's notes could previously detach the draft from its tag, so the next run couldn't find it and created a second draft instead of updating the first. The update now keeps the tag attached, so re-running against the same release updates the one draft instead of creating another.
- **Exit status on partial failure:** A run where one or more requested audiences failed to render previously still reported success and could overwrite an existing changelog.json with partial results. Chartula now exits with a failure status whenever an audience fails, writes only what rendered successfully, and leaves existing output untouched if nothing rendered at all.
- **Missing API key:** Running against Anthropic without an API key previously let the run fetch pull requests and fail only later, with a raw error on every audience. Chartula now checks for the key at startup and refuses with a clear configuration error before any GitHub request is made.
- **Angle brackets in changelog text:** Text written by the model that included angle brackets outside of code formatting, such as a filename like release-\<tag>.md, could previously break the Markdown rendering of CHANGELOG.md, release notes and the customer release page. These are now escaped automatically wherever they appear outside a code span, so such text always renders correctly.
- **Faithfulness check accuracy:** The thorough faithfulness check previously could flag a pull request reference in the generated text as unsupported, since it wasn't given that reference among the facts to check against. The check now receives each pull request's number and link, so real references are no longer flagged incorrectly.
- **Truncated faithfulness checks:** If the model's context window was too small to receive the full facts during a faithfulness check, it could still return a clean, well-formed verdict despite never having seen the content, reporting zero problems instead of surfacing the real failure. Chartula now detects when the reported input size can't match what was sent and fails the run instead of reporting a false-clean result.
- **Customer changelog outcomes:** Customer changelog entries could previously restate or negate what changed instead of saying what it means for you, such as saying a bug's cause is gone rather than what you no longer have to do about it. Entries now draw that outcome from the underlying change's facts, so they state an actual benefit instead of repeating the change itself.
- **User-visible change detection:** Every change typed as a feature was previously treated as visible to you, even purely internal ones like a file format change, so customer changelogs could include changes you'd never actually encounter. Visibility is now decided by a label a reviewer attaches to the pull request, falling back to its category only when no label says otherwise.
- **Setting entries in changelogs:** An entry about a configurable setting could previously name only where to change it, without ever saying what choosing it actually gets you. Such entries now state the benefit first, with where to find the setting mentioned afterward.
- **Customer changelog cutoffs:** The customer changelog could previously come out completely empty, with no error reported, because the model's extended reasoning used up its entire output budget before it wrote any text. The output budget has been doubled, leaving enough room for the model to finish writing after it reasons.
- **Empty customer changelogs:** When the model's entire answer was just the release description, that description could previously be lifted out as metadata, leaving an empty changelog body and no release page, with no error reported. The description is now only extracted when there's actual content left behind it, so a genuine answer is no longer discarded.
- **Required changelog outcomes:** Customer changelog entries could previously leave out what a change means for you entirely, since the instructions allowed that part to be dropped. Every entry now must state that outcome, so you always learn what you can rely on from a change, not only what changed.
- **Customer changelog shape:** Customer changelog entries previously varied in structure from run to run, sometimes repeating a contributor-only expression no end user would recognize, closing with a restated change rather than its outcome, or opening on the work that was done. Entries now follow a fixed shape, grouped and ordered consistently, naming a setting's location when relevant, and built only from facts and language you'd actually encounter.
- **Unreadable faithfulness checks:** If the model's response during the thorough faithfulness check couldn't be read, the check previously reported the same result as a clean pass with zero findings, even though nothing had actually been verified. The run summary and any flagged passages now say when a check came back unreadable instead of looking identical to one that found nothing wrong.
- **Breaking-change flags:** The free, rule-based check previously flagged any mention of the word breaking as a false claim, even in ordinary prose describing a setting or the check itself. That check no longer looks for breaking-change claims at all; the thorough check catches real ones instead when it's enabled, though with it disabled there is no check for this.
- **LLM usage reporting:** A call to the model that reported no token usage at all previously looked the same as one that simply used very few tokens. Chartula now tells the two apart, so run metrics stay accurate.
- **Truncated output and false breaking flags:** Generated changelog text could previously be cut off mid-sentence with no error reported, because no output limit was sent to the model and the provider silently used a very small default; separately, a change whose description merely discussed breaking changes, rather than declaring one, could be mislabeled as breaking. Output now always carries a configurable limit to avoid truncation, and breaking changes are detected only from the exact Conventional Commits footer rather than any mention of the words.
